evidence: Kraftwerk set up the Kling Klang studio in 1970 at Mintropstrasse 16 in Düsseldorf and treated it as the band's real beginning. They recorded on their own tape machines and took masters elsewhere for final mixing, which let them produce themselves. From 1976 they recorded 'Trans-Europe Express' there using custom-built Synthanorma sequencers. Kling Klang became their own label imprint in 1975, distributed by EMI and later Warner (Wikipedia's Kling Klang article).

trackPair.whatToListenFor: 'Autobahn' drifts: synthesisers, flute and voices float over a loose pulse for more than twenty minutes. 'Trans-Europe Express' is locked tight, a repeating sequence clanking forward like wheels on rails, with every part in its place. The difference is a band that now owned its room and could spend as long as it liked getting a pattern exactly right.

explanation: Kling Klang was Kraftwerk's own studio in Düsseldorf, and later the name of their own record label. As a label it mattered for ownership: from 1975 Kraftwerk owned their own recordings and set their own release pace. The effect on the music ran through the studio of the same name. Because they owned the room, they could produce themselves, have custom instruments built and work slowly in a way no booked commercial studio would allow, and from 1976 they made 'Trans-Europe Express' there with custom-built sequencers; its precision is the result. 'Autobahn' is paired as the before, because Conny Plank co-produced it, which has its own connection on the map.
